chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Hashimi, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Khul' (mutual divorce) wife, the Mubar'ah (divorce by mutual consent with compensation) wife, and the Musta'marah (divorce by request) wife do not inherit anything from the husband in their divorce if that divorce was initiated by them during the husband's illness, and even if he dies, because the bond of marriage has been severed from them and from him. Therefore, the correct interpretation of this report is to restrict it to those specifically named in the report as Khul', Mubar'ah, and Musta'marah wives, because the cause for this ruling is on their part due to their request for divorce, unlike the Mutlaqah (simply divorced) wife who does not request it, but may even be reluctant to it. And upon this basis, there is no contradiction between the reports.

key_terms.الْمُبَارِئَةُ: A wife who initiates Mubar'ah (divorce by mutual consent)
key_terms.الْمُخْتَلِعَةُ: A wife who initiates Khul' (divorce by mutual consent, usually with financial compensation)
key_terms.الْمُسْتَأْمَرَةُ: A wife who requests divorce from the husband
key_terms.الْمُطَلَّقَةُ: A wife who is simply divorced by the husband without her initiating it

ai.seo_question: Do wives who initiate divorce during the husband's illness inherit from him?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi presents this narration to resolve apparent contradictions in inheritance laws by distinguishing between wives who initiate divorce (Khul', Mubar'ah, Musta'marah) and those passively divorced (Mutlaqah). The ruling that initiators do not inherit stems from the principle that the 'bond of chastity' (Ismah) is severed by their specific claim for divorce during the husband's illness, a nuance that aligns with Shia juristic methodology of reconciling conflicting reports through contextual specification.
